title: Why culture matters in leading DHS work
objective: See how culture shapes DHS work and choose your own starting point privately.
learn: Explore how culture influences who finds an opening, how a notice is read, how a meeting feels and who trusts an agency. Use developmental models to select a private practice goal.

teaching.title: Find the decision within the routine
teaching.text: Picture the last time someone said, “Let me know if you have concerns.” Who could reach that person? How soon was silence treated as permission to proceed? The invitation, the channel and the deadline are all decisions. Someone with authority chose them, even if the team has used them for years.

teaching.title: Give the team’s culture a name
teaching.text: In a Minnesota public agency, a work group might value direct self-advocacy and also soften disagreement to keep a meeting cordial. New staff must figure out when to speak plainly and when plain speech will sound too forceful. An experienced colleague can make that expectation visible and help the team change it.

teaching.title: Choose an entry point
teaching.text: The Intercultural Development Continuum describes ways people make meaning of cultural difference. The Intercultural Development Inventory is an assessment associated with that model. In these lessons you can privately consider your response to a decision. Start with a decision you can influence, then follow its effect on someone with less control.

teaching.title: Read the two maps accurately
teaching.text: Bennett’s Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity describes six stages: Denial, Defense, Minimization, Acceptance, Adaptation and Integration. The Intercultural Development Continuum describes five orientations: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. The course units give you practice, and no decision here produces an IDI score. Choose the lesson that will help you with a real situation.

scenario: A program team is changing the public callback hour. A clerk has heard from callers who share phones. The manager intends to announce the change on Friday and invites final thoughts at a Thursday staff meeting. The clerk works the evening shift.
decision: Which step could an aspiring leader take before the schedule goes out?

choices.label: Forward the invitation to the evening shift.
choices.feedback: That supplies notice. Thursday’s meeting still determines whose evidence reaches the manager in time.

choices.label: Bring an anonymized account of the missed calls and ask for a decision window both shifts can use.
choices.feedback: The manager can examine a service consequence before acting. The clerk gets a way to correct the account, and the team can explain its eventual decision.

choices.label: Recommend sticking with the old hour.
choices.feedback: That may protect current callers. It also settles the matter before hearing whose access might improve under a different schedule.

perspective: In this fictional case, the evening clerk says, “People have told me they can use the shared phone only after the other person gets home. I could have brought those examples before Friday if I'd known a decision was due.” Imagine you share a phone. What information would let you choose a workable callback time without explaining your household arrangement to everyone?
reconsider: The team can publish a decision date, receive evening input and still meet its deadline.
followup: Compare which concerns reached the manager with the reasons the team records for the final schedule.
reflection: Which routine at your desk turns someone’s silence into a workplace decision?
transfer: Write a private two-line decision log naming who can offer evidence and when your team could still act on it.

sources.title: Intercultural Development Continuum
Milton Bennett · A developmental approach to training for intercultural sensitivity

title: Who DHS serves
objective: Describe the communities your unit serves and respond when someone says knowing them does not matter.
learn: The communities DHS serves, including the 11 Tribal Nations, newer and long-established communities, rural Minnesotans, languages spoken and people with disabilities.

teaching.title: Know whom the records leave out
teaching.text: Service data describe the people and events a system has recorded. A low number of completed applications in a rural county could reflect population, eligibility, travel or barriers before an application gets opened. A useful first question is which part of the process produced the number.

teaching.title: Distinguish relationships
teaching.text: Minnesota law recognizes a government-to-government relationship with eleven federally recognized Tribal Nations sharing geography with the state. A community provider, an individual Tribal citizen and a Tribal government can each contribute different knowledge. Formal consultation has its own scope and channels. An open town hall cannot stand in for those relationships.

teaching.title: Ask about access locally
teaching.text: Consider rural residents without reliable connectivity, people who use a communication device, recent arrivals and long-established communities. Each label covers many circumstances. Ask affected people and relevant partners which part of the proposed change they can evaluate, how they prefer to participate and what authority the agency actually holds.

teaching.title: Answer the objection about knowing communities
teaching.text: A colleague says, “If we treat everyone consistently, why learn about the communities here?” A useful reply begins with the actual program. For example, “We need people to receive the same information in time. Without learning which formats and languages reach people in our service area, we cannot tell whether that is happening.” Compare what local public information can establish with what you still need to ask.

scenario: A director wants to move a regional information session online. A sign-in sheet from last year includes service providers, two county workers and no residents who identified a need for interpretation. A staff member treats that as sufficient evidence to proceed in English.
decision: What would give the director a firmer basis for choosing a format?

choices.label: Ask providers to represent all the people they serve.
choices.feedback: Providers can describe patterns they see, but they cannot authorize a Tribal government position or speak for people who have never reached their service.

choices.label: Offer the same online session statewide and compare turnout.
choices.feedback: Turnout will describe people able to attend. It gives little evidence about those the format excluded.

choices.label: Map who could be affected, check applicable Tribal channels and offer more than one way for residents to respond.
choices.feedback: This gives the director separate evidence about public access, service partners and any government-to-government obligations.

perspective: In this fictional case, a resident who missed last year's event says, “My neighbor showed me the notice after the meeting. I would have asked for an interpreter if I'd known I could come.” Who is absent before an attendance count begins? What would they have to spend, disclose or arrange to be counted?
reconsider: The immediate task is to identify what decision is still open and the proper partners for it.
followup: Publish how input changed the format and offer a route for corrections before the session.
reflection: Where has a contact list in your work become a substitute for knowing whom a service affects?
transfer: Redraw one invitation list with separate entries for people using the service, community partners and governments where applicable.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes §10.65 · Government-to-government relationship with Tribal governments
Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices

title: Same rule, different experience
objective: Trace how one process lands differently for different people.
learn: How language, disability, internet access, work schedules, transportation and past experience with government change who meets a deadline.

teaching.title: Draw the two clocks
teaching.text: A team may count from the moment a notice leaves its system. A person can act only after receiving it in a usable form, understanding what is needed and being able to get help. Write down when each event happens. A deadline with a single date can create very different response windows.

teaching.title: Check the source of the deadline
teaching.text: A statute, a program rule and an office habit give staff different room to act. Verify which part is fixed with the responsible owner. A supervisor who cannot change a filing date may still influence when a reminder goes out, how it is worded, and which channels are usable.

teaching.title: Measure usable time
teaching.text: Record timestamps already authorized for the purpose. Look for time lost between dispatch and usable contact as well as the final return rate. A small set of voluntary accounts can explain an unexpected pattern while avoiding disclosure of personal information beyond what the review needs.

teaching.title: Map the work a notice assumes
teaching.text: An online return may assume reliable internet and a device that works with the form. A visit to the counter may assume transportation, paid time off and trust that bringing a question will be safe. Asking for a different format can consume part of a response window. Choose one of these possible explanations, then identify who could verify it.

scenario: A team sends a Friday afternoon reminder for records due Tuesday. One person receives it electronically on Friday, another gets a mailed copy on Monday, and another receives requested language assistance on Tuesday. All three records show the same reminder date.
decision: What do you change first?

choices.label: Ask the deadline owner which parts are flexible and test earlier reminders in the requested formats.
choices.feedback: This distinguishes the governing date from a local habit. Compare how much usable time people gain and whether staff create another delay.

choices.label: Waive the date for everyone who requests it.
choices.feedback: This may exceed your authority. It also places the burden on people to identify an available exception.

choices.label: Make the reminder more urgent.
choices.feedback: A clearer reminder could help someone who already has it. It cannot restore days spent waiting for a usable copy.

perspective: In this fictional case, the person who received language assistance explains, “Tuesday was the first day I knew which records you needed. I had to ask another office for one of them.” If you receive information on the final day, what would an office need to explain before asking why you missed the deadline?
reconsider: A deadline may be fixed while the team’s own timing remains within its control.
followup: Track usable hours and ask whether earlier contact introduced a new access problem.
reflection: Whose time does your team’s timeline currently record?
transfer: Sketch the sending, receiving and acting dates for one routine exchange. Mark the first step your role can influence.

sources.title: Institute for Healthcare Improvement · Testing changes

title: Difference on your own team
objective: Respond well to requests about names, holidays and faith practices.
learn: How staff experience the same workplace differently, and how to hold a curiosity conversation with open questions.

teaching.title: Ask a question a person can decline
teaching.text: Ask how a colleague would like their name said or displayed in the setting you share. Offer a private way to answer. A person may use different forms in different contexts. Public correction repeatedly puts the cost of teaching on the person whose name was missed.

teaching.title: Separate coordination from disclosure
teaching.text: Teams need dates, coverage and a reliable way to hand work off. Most scheduling decisions can begin with those needs. Asking a colleague to establish the importance of a holiday in front of the group turns a schedule discussion into a judgment about identity or belief.

teaching.title: Model the correction yourself
teaching.text: When you mispronounce a name, briefly acknowledge it, use the preferred pronunciation and move on. When peers call a holiday event a team commitment, name the actual work requirement and clarify how people can participate in team life on other occasions. Leaders give everyone permission to change course.

teaching.title: Prepare a practical response to a faith-related request
teaching.text: If a colleague raises a schedule conflict connected with a faith practice, ask what adjustment they are seeking and how they would like to discuss it. Use current workplace procedures and the appropriate human resources contact when a formal accommodation may be involved. Keep coverage planning distinct from a judgment about the sincerity or importance of a belief.

scenario: A supervisor asks who wants to cover a winter office gathering. A new employee quietly declines. A colleague says the person is not making an effort to fit in, and the supervisor is about to use participation as evidence of teamwork.
decision: How do you respond?

choices.label: Ask the employee to explain their reasons at the next team meeting.
choices.feedback: This puts a private decision on display and makes acceptance depend on an explanation.

choices.label: Assess teamwork through work evidence and offer a private conversation about participation preferences.
choices.feedback: You keep the work standard clear and allow the employee to decide what to share. Check whether the event was the team’s only chance to build relationships.

choices.label: Stop inviting the person to future activities.
choices.feedback: This solves an immediate awkward moment by reducing opportunities. The person may want invitations and the freedom to decide each time.

perspective: In this fictional case, the employee says privately, “I can take my turn covering the service desk. I didn't know that declining a social event would be counted against me.” What might an employee reasonably fear about saying no when a supervisor organizes the event?
reconsider: An aspiring leader can interrupt the inference about teamwork even without controlling the performance review.
followup: Look at later work examples and who gets informal access to colleagues.
reflection: Which optional activity in your workplace is quietly treated as evidence of commitment?
transfer: Draft a one-sentence invitation with the work expectation and the choice plainly separated.

sources.title: Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams

title: Curiosity before conclusions
objective: Catch an assumption before it becomes a judgment.
learn: Practice Describe, Interpret, Evaluate. Separate what you saw, the meaning you supplied and how that meaning affected your judgment.

teaching.title: Describe
teaching.text: Record the smallest observation you could defend. “After I offered the first time slot, Taylor was quiet for several seconds” is more useful than “Taylor was reluctant.” The first account leaves room for the person to say they were checking a calendar or waiting for a support person.

teaching.title: Interpret, then seek evidence
teaching.text: Generate more than one explanation, including one about the office’s own behavior. As a leader, ask what evidence would distinguish them. Experimental research on getting another person’s perspective suggests asking directly can produce information that imagining their answer does not provide.

teaching.title: Make evaluation provisional
teaching.text: You still have to decide what happens next. Explain what you understood, invite correction in a usable way, and say what will happen after that. A private follow-up or a choice of response channels can make an honest correction easier when the other person depends on the service.

scenario: In a disability service discussion, Lee nods as the worker outlines a change. The note taker enters “agreed.” Moments later Lee sends a message asking when the previous support would stop.
decision: What should the worker establish before finalizing the note?

choices.label: Treat the nod as provisional approval and proceed unless Lee objects.
choices.feedback: Provisional approval still puts the burden on Lee to overturn a decision that was never clearly expressed.

choices.label: Ask Lee why they did not say no at the meeting.
choices.feedback: The question assumes a refusal and could make Lee responsible for a misunderstanding.

choices.label: Ask what Lee understood and which option they want, then check the wording of the note.
choices.feedback: The worker can distinguish hearing, understanding and choosing. Leave the outcome open until Lee’s answer is known.

perspective: In this fictional case, Lee adds, “I nodded because I heard the proposal. I still need to know what happens to my current support before I choose.” From Lee’s position, what phrase would signal that a real choice remains available?
reconsider: A smile, nod or silence has no single meaning. A person can understand a proposal and still disagree with it.
followup: Document what Lee chooses, the follow-up they request and any point still open.
reflection: When have you supplied a motive where you had only an observation?
transfer: Rewrite one fictional case note using three sentences for the observation, the unanswered question and the next action.

sources.title: Eyal, Steffel and Epley · Perspective mistaking
Minnesota · Person-centered, informed choice and transition protocol

title: When difference feels like a threat
objective: Recognize us-versus-them thinking and reframe it without shaming.
learn: How stress, scarcity and change fuel us-versus-them talk, and how to steer it back to the people served.

teaching.title: Identify the stake
teaching.text: When a service queue grows, staff may hear a request for more time as a threat to the people still waiting. Name the stake explicitly. Acknowledging the queue can lower defensiveness enough for the team to examine why this particular request is being treated as the problem.

teaching.title: Inspect the explanation
teaching.text: A claim such as “they expect special treatment” supplies a motive with no evidence. Ask which step took longer, what information was available and whether staff controlled the delay. Do not ask a colleague who shares a background with the person to supply an explanation.

teaching.title: Keep two outcomes visible
teaching.text: Identify measures for both the pressure staff feel and the service consequence. If speed improves while people leave without understanding their options, the team may have transferred its burden to people outside the office. Give staff a way to report both outcomes safely.

scenario: A unit’s line runs late. A person asks to have an explanation repeated through an interpreter. An experienced worker says others should not have to wait because one household is “demanding.” You coordinate the counter today.
decision: How would you use the next minute?

choices.label: Acknowledge the wait, arrange coverage if available and give the person time for their question.
choices.feedback: You address the operational pressure and preserve the service conversation. Later the supervisor can examine scheduling and the unsupported claim about motive.

choices.label: Ask the person to return on a quieter day.
choices.feedback: Another visit may be costly and may not be feasible. Check the person’s preference and the program’s responsibilities before changing their access.

choices.label: Challenge the worker publicly until they retract the comment.
choices.feedback: The remark warrants follow-up. A prolonged public dispute may expose the person and leave both the immediate access need and the queue unattended.

perspective: In this fictional case, the person at the counter tells the interpreter, “The first explanation gave me a date. I still need to know what to bring. Otherwise I'll have to come back and wait again.” What might a person hear if a discussion about queue length happens within their hearing?
reconsider: You can separate a legitimate staffing concern from an unverified explanation for a person’s request.
followup: Check how long coverage took, whether the person got a usable answer and what contributed to the backlog.
reflection: Which pressures make your team quickest to assign blame?
transfer: Write a two-sentence response that acknowledges a constraint and keeps a service option open.

sources.title: HHS Office of Minority Health · National CLAS Standards
Eyal, Steffel and Epley · Perspective mistaking

title: What we share
objective: Find a shared goal when staff from different backgrounds disagree and confirm what that goal means to the person served.
learn: Explore possible shared concerns such as safety, dignity, being heard and caring for family. Ask each participant which concern matters here and what it would look like in practice.

teaching.title: Clarify the shared word
teaching.text: Ask each person what they would see if safety or dignity improved. One participant might mean knowing a provider will arrive. Another might mean being able to choose who enters their home. Those accounts can overlap, and either can reveal a missed design requirement.

teaching.title: Identify who holds the choice
teaching.text: A supervisor can decide how staff schedule a conversation. The person receiving support may be directing a different decision about their own life. Name the decision on the table and who has authority over each part before trying to reach agreement.

teaching.title: Check which burden remains
teaching.text: A common aim can speed up a group conversation, but agreement on the aim can also hide an unequal cost. Ask who would have to take time off, give up privacy or ask again if the preferred arrangement fails. Record the remaining issue in concrete terms.

teaching.title: Use the same method between colleagues
teaching.text: One employee wants every follow-up booked during a call. Another wants time for people to consult someone they trust. Both may care about avoiding loss of service. Ask each colleague what evidence would show the person could act on the next step. Then invite the person to choose the arrangement that works for them within the actual requirements.

scenario: A DSD worker and an adult planning supports both want a reliable start to the workday. The worker proposes the same early check-in every weekday. The person says shifts rotate and a text the prior evening would let them decide.
decision: What is the best next question?

choices.label: Can we agree that a fixed schedule is the safest choice?
choices.feedback: The question turns the worker’s preferred method into the meaning of safety before testing it.

choices.label: Which mornings cause the difficulty, how would you like to confirm a shift, and what should happen if plans change?
choices.feedback: This turns the shared aim into a plan the person can evaluate and gives the worker a way to check service feasibility.

choices.label: Should we put this off until the schedule becomes predictable?
choices.feedback: The person has described a workable direction now. Waiting may leave a present access problem unaddressed.

perspective: In this fictional case, the person explains, “I check my shifts when tomorrow's schedule comes out. A message then lets me choose a time, and you can see that I confirmed it.” What could a reliable start look like to the person that a punctuality measure alone would miss?
reconsider: In the person-centered planning context, confirm who the person wants involved and how they want to communicate.
followup: Review a small number of actual mornings with the person’s agreement and ask if the arrangement worked for them.
reflection: Which word in your team’s purpose statement would benefit from a concrete definition by people served?
transfer: Complete the sentence “We both want ___, and we still need to decide ___.”

sources.title: Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices
Minnesota · Person-centered, informed choice and transition protocol

title: Every group has strengths and blind spots
objective: See your own culture and others' without idealizing or condemning either.
learn: Why making up for past harm by withholding honest feedback is unfair, and how to give the same honest feedback to everyone.

teaching.title: Describe the benefit in context
teaching.text: A fast verbal handoff can work well when two colleagues overlap and the facts are settled. A written handoff can help when the next shift needs a trail or has time to check details. Both practices carry costs. Ask what each team was trying to protect.

teaching.title: Look for whose work becomes visible
teaching.text: Day staff may resolve issues in a meeting leaders attend. Evening staff may leave careful records of problems they prevented. The supervisor sees a different sample of each shift’s work. Visibility alone cannot establish judgment, readiness or commitment.

teaching.title: Invite disagreement about the standard
teaching.text: Share examples of work that led to a better outcome and ask each shift what the current review misses. Offer a way to respond outside the group, especially when supervisors evaluate the people giving feedback. Then decide what evidence should travel with an assignment or review.

teaching.title: Offer honest feedback across backgrounds
teaching.text: Withholding correction to avoid hurting a colleague can deny them information others receive. In this handoff case, identify the missing step and its consequence, ask what got in the way, and give a chance to practice the revised method. Apply that work standard to both shifts. Ask about each person’s preferred feedback channel privately rather than inferring it from identity.

scenario: Day staff describe evening colleagues as overly cautious. Evening staff describe the day team as careless. A supervisor must decide what makes a strong handoff before naming a project lead.
decision: What evidence should guide the decision?

choices.label: Use whichever team closes more items in a shift.
choices.feedback: Volume is useful, but case mix, overlap and reopened items could explain the difference.

choices.label: Have the two shifts vote on which procedure to use.
choices.feedback: A vote gives larger or better represented groups a built-in advantage and may overlook the evidence behind both routines.

choices.label: Compare matched handoffs, including what later had to be redone, and ask both shifts what each record leaves out.
choices.feedback: This tests both claims against comparable work and reveals which successful actions were previously invisible.

perspective: In this fictional case, an evening employee says, “By the time we get a referral, the person who approved it has gone home. Recording what we checked lets the next shift pick it up.” What kind of good judgment would never be noticed by someone watching only daytime meetings?
reconsider: A work group’s successful habit can have a blind spot without making every person in the group behave the same way.
followup: Publish the revised handoff standard with examples from both shifts and revisit it after a short test.
reflection: Whose readiness would your usual evidence make easiest to recognize?
transfer: Name one piece of evidence you currently see and a comparable one a less visible team could supply.

sources.title: Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams
Institute for Healthcare Improvement · Testing changes

title: Disagreeing without dividing
objective: Keep a heated conversation respectful and safe to speak in.
learn: How to set and use group agreements, and how respect, responsibility and communication work together during conflict.

teaching.title: Separate the claim from its delivery
teaching.text: Ask participants to state the decision, the evidence and the consequence they see. A direct challenge and a carefully qualified concern can both contain important information. Polished delivery can also conceal a weak claim. Make evidence available for examination in more than one format.

teaching.title: Keep dissent available
teaching.text: A working agreement can specify how to request a pause, submit a correction after the meeting or record a dissenting reason. The leader should show what happens when someone uses the agreement. A written invitation carries little weight if previous challengers heard nothing back.

teaching.title: Close the loop
teaching.text: The decision maker can explain what changed, which concern remains, and who can reopen the decision if new evidence arrives. If no change was possible, give the reason and identify the actual limit. Agreement is an unreliable measure of whether people had meaningful influence.

scenario: A team is redesigning a public intake greeting. A worker says bluntly that the wording is confusing; another says quietly that clients might prefer the old wording. The chair hears conflict and proposes moving on.
decision: What could the chair do in the next two minutes?

choices.label: Ask each person about the part that confuses people, agree on a quick comparison and name who will decide.
choices.feedback: This protects disagreement while turning it into a test. Ask whether a private correction would surface evidence people cannot share in the room.

choices.label: Ask both workers to use a more positive tone before taking up the issue.
choices.feedback: This may improve surface comfort while withholding a hearing from people who have evidence about a public barrier.

choices.label: Seek unanimous agreement before trying any wording.
choices.feedback: Unanimity can hide quiet pressure and delay a reversible test. Describe what feedback can change instead.

perspective: In this fictional case, after the meeting, the quieter worker explains, “I saw two callers hesitate at that line. I wanted us to try the new greeting with someone before we chose it.” What would someone at the lowest rank need to see next time before believing dissent was welcome?
reconsider: Different preferences about directness or emotional expression are possibilities to check with each person.
followup: Log which concern the test addressed and return the result to the people who raised it.
reflection: When did a conversation end peacefully while a significant concern remained unresolved?
transfer: Write a closing sentence that names the owner, the open issue and the route for later evidence.

sources.title: Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams
Eyal, Steffel and Epley · Perspective mistaking

title: Your own culture, made visible
objective: Name the unwritten rules of your team and workplace.
learn: The values, habits and history behind your sense of "normal," including Minnesota workplace culture and DHS's unwritten rules.

teaching.title: Find your own starting point
teaching.text: How did you learn whether it was acceptable to question a supervisor, arrive after a meeting began or call a director by a first name? A rule can feel natural because you have practiced it for years. Someone with equal skill may have learned a different way to show respect.

teaching.title: Locate majority power
teaching.text: Historically dominant white American and Minnesota workplace expectations can influence what an agency rewards as professionalism, confidence or cooperation. An individual white Minnesotan may hold quite different expectations. To investigate your team’s culture, identify an actual reward or penalty and what behavior triggered it.

teaching.title: Read an informal phrase both ways
teaching.text: Consider a supervisor who ends a meeting with “That should work.” An insider might recognize polite hesitation. A new colleague might enter an approval in the project record. The supervisor can make the decision explicit and offer a private route to question it, reducing reliance on insider knowledge.

scenario: A unit offers short acting assignments to employees who ask the director after a meeting. Staff describe the process as open to anyone. The evening shift does not attend, and some day staff understand approaching a director without invitation as an overstep.
decision: What could make the hidden rule visible and change access?

choices.label: Coach the evening shift to introduce themselves to the director.
choices.feedback: Introductions may help individuals while leaving the time and selection process intact.

choices.label: Publish how to express interest on both shifts, what evidence counts and when decisions will be made.
choices.feedback: This makes the opportunity visible and gives the supervisor a way to see whether interest from a new source is actually considered.

choices.label: Have staff anonymously rate the director’s approachability.
choices.feedback: The result could signal an issue, but would not tell applicants how to reach a specific opening.

perspective: In this fictional case, an employee explains, “The posting says requests go through my supervisor. When the day team spoke with the director, I thought they already had permission I didn't have.” If a person has never seen an acting assignment announced, what reason would they have to ask for one?
reconsider: Aspirants can identify a missed route to opportunity. Selection and a fair process still need an owner with the right authority.
followup: Compare who heard about the next opening in time and which experiences the panel counted.
reflection: Which piece of insider knowledge made your own first year at work easier?
transfer: Describe the same opportunity twice, first as an insider understands it, then as a newcomer could actually find it.

sources.title: Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams

title: When the same is not fair
objective: Find who falls through a practice that treats everyone identically.
learn: The difference between identical treatment and fair access, and how neutral rules can produce unequal results.

teaching.title: Identify the actual requirement
teaching.text: For example, a team may need to establish that a person received important information. Requiring a return phone call at a particular hour is one possible method. Check with the process owner which parts the program requires, what alternatives are authorized, and what would have to be protected in any change.

teaching.title: Count those who fall out
teaching.text: The number of people who completed the call tells you little about people who tried and could not get through. Ask what the call system records about attempts, disconnections and hours. Where records are incomplete, invite an account from someone affected and acknowledge the gap.

teaching.title: Test a comparable route
teaching.text: Maintain the same underlying service standard across channels. If someone chooses written communication, identify how to confirm receipt, ask questions and correct a misunderstanding. Check whether the alternative moves delay to another worker or creates a privacy concern.

scenario: A team counts every unanswered morning callback as one attempt to reach a person. Three missed calls trigger a review. Someone working overnight says all three calls came while they slept, despite a request for afternoon contact.
decision: What could you test within the team’s authority?

choices.label: Check the current contact rules and offer a confirmed callback window, then review successful contact and repeat attempts.
choices.feedback: This tests the actual purpose of the calls while preserving any required steps and giving the person a say in timing.

choices.label: Ask every person to explain their work schedule before the first call.
choices.feedback: Some may want to say only when contact is possible. A preference can be sufficient and less intrusive.

choices.label: Increase the number of morning attempts.
choices.feedback: More attempts can consume staff time while reproducing the same scheduling barrier.

perspective: In this fictional case, the overnight worker tells the office, “I left an afternoon number with intake. The messages went to that number in the morning, when I had the ringer off.” How would you describe the difference between “we tried three times” and “we reached the person in a way they could use”?
reconsider: Identical treatment can yield unequal usable access. The review should also account for people who could not respond at all.
followup: Review contact success alongside waiting time, failed attempts and staff time over a small test.
reflection: What equal-treatment rule protects a real purpose in your work? Where might its implementation drift?
transfer: Specify one baseline, one authorized alternative and one unintended effect to watch.

sources.title: Institute for Healthcare Improvement · Testing changes
Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices

title: Patterns of difference
objective: Use cultural patterns as starting questions, never as profiles.
learn: Direct and indirect communication, individual and family decisions, time, hierarchy and trust, and why averages never describe the person in front of you.

teaching.title: Use patterns to widen the inquiry
teaching.text: A person may avoid interrupting a specialist, prefer to decide with family, or want a clear answer alone. Directness can change with language, stakes, setting or trust. A leader can use these possibilities to offer an opening without predicting which one fits.

teaching.title: Ask about the specific decision
teaching.text: Try asking, “Who would you like involved when we discuss the options?” Follow with “How would you like to let us know what you decide?” Those questions give room for changing preferences. Asking what people of a particular background usually do puts one person in the role of spokesperson.

teaching.title: Give time a concrete meaning
teaching.text: “Soon” may leave an employee guessing whether the leader means today or next month. For a service decision, state an actual date, check whether it works and explain which parts can change. A person can accept the timing while still wanting to discuss the proposal privately.

scenario: A worker concludes someone agrees because they speak softly, smile and say they will discuss the proposal at home. The worker plans to close the case that afternoon.
decision: Which response recognizes the pattern and preserves choice?

choices.label: Ask a colleague who shares the person’s language what the smile means.
choices.feedback: A colleague may help with language access but cannot determine this person’s intent from a smile.

choices.label: Wait indefinitely until the family contacts the office.
choices.feedback: Waiting passes the work of reopening the case to the person and leaves deadlines unclear.

choices.label: Ask what the person wants to consider, whom they want involved and when they would like the team to check back.
choices.feedback: These questions establish how the person wants to decide and prevent the team from turning a social cue into a service choice.

perspective: In this fictional case, the person tells the worker, “I understood the offer. I want to compare what changes at home before I decide. When can I give you an answer?” What would you want the worker to say if your smile meant you had heard them and were still thinking?
reconsider: A communication style belongs to a situation as well as a person. Ask again when the stakes or participants change.
followup: Record the agreed follow-up date and leave the substantive choice open until the person confirms it.
reflection: Which cue do you most often treat as agreement at work?
transfer: Write an open question about time, hierarchy or disagreement that contains no guess about identity.

sources.title: Eyal, Steffel and Epley · Perspective mistaking
Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices

title: Disability as culture and identity
objective: Redesign a meeting so the person served leads it.
learn: Disability culture and Deaf culture, ableism, and why people with disabilities know their own needs best.

teaching.title: Recognize identity and expertise
teaching.text: Deaf and disability communities include people with distinct histories, languages and ways of identifying. Some Deaf people identify with a linguistic and cultural community. Others describe their identities differently. Check the person’s own terms and access preferences without assuming a language or communication method from a label.

teaching.title: Notice ableism in an ordinary meeting
teaching.text: A fast round of questions can privilege speech, immediate processing and the ability to interrupt. Staff may then give greater weight to a family member who answers quickly. A leader can send options in advance, build in time for communication and ask the person whom they want beside them.

teaching.title: Give the person control over support
teaching.text: Informed choice includes choosing help to deliberate or communicate. Ask which parts a support person should help with. Address the person directly and agree on how they will indicate a decision or request more time. If legal decision authority matters, verify its actual scope through the proper channel.

scenario: Sam uses a communication device and asks an aunt to explain the timing of transport. The planner turns to the aunt for all remaining decisions. Sam types a question about evening activities while the team starts to pack up.
decision: How should the planner repair the meeting?

choices.label: Restart only after Sam can attend without family.
choices.feedback: That would remove the support Sam chose and make independence a condition for being heard.

choices.label: Return to Sam’s question, ask what the aunt should help with, and wait for Sam to indicate what happens next.
choices.feedback: The person can direct the decision using support. Confirm how the team will share the outcome for correction.

choices.label: Let the aunt finish, then send a standard copy of the plan.
choices.feedback: A later copy is useful, but it cannot restore an opportunity to shape options that were already closed.

perspective: In this fictional case, Sam types, “My aunt knows when the van comes. I want to tell you which evening activities matter to me. Can we finish that part before everyone leaves?” Sam asked for help with one part of the discussion. Where did staff expand that request into authority over the whole meeting?
reconsider: A person may want others to help weigh options and still direct the choice. The meeting’s pace and turn-taking should support that distinction.
followup: Ask Sam whether the written account reflects the choice and whether the next meeting should run differently.
reflection: Whose communication speed sets the pace of a meeting you lead?
transfer: Draw a three-turn agenda that identifies who opens the decision, how supporters contribute and how the person can correct the record.

sources.title: National Association of the Deaf · Community and culture
Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices
Minnesota · Person-centered, informed choice and transition protocol

title: Values in tension
objective: Decide how to respect a family's values while meeting a legal duty.
learn: Distinguish unfamiliarity from a concrete safety concern. Ask about the person’s wishes and seek authorized consultation where a legal or safety duty may apply.

teaching.title: Hear the preference in the person’s terms
teaching.text: Ask whom the person wants in the conversation, which part they want help with and how they want staff to check back. A preference to consult family can express self-direction. Staff cannot infer agreement to a particular plan from someone’s wish to have family present.

teaching.title: Keep your evidence straight
teaching.text: Record what the person said or showed, the specific concern that arose and the information you still lack. A practice unfamiliar to staff is a reason for inquiry. Evidence of harm or an applicable duty requires attention through the authorized process. One cannot be inferred from the other.

teaching.title: Seek timely consultation
teaching.text: If confidentiality, safety, consent or a reporting obligation may be involved, consult the appropriate current program guidance and authorized staff. Act within any applicable timelines. Explain what you can to the person in a way they can use. Staff should avoid promising secrecy or outcomes beyond their control. For an adult who meets Minnesota’s vulnerable-adult definition, a mandated reporter with reason to believe maltreatment occurred has an immediate reporting duty under section 626.557. The statute describes applicable exceptions and authorized reporting routes. Ask for help interpreting a duty promptly and carry out any immediate duty on time.

scenario: An adult asks for a sister to help discuss a change at home. During the conversation the person sends a private message asking how to raise a safety concern. The family expects to hear the plan together today.
decision: How should the worker handle the private message?

choices.label: Treat the request for privacy as a rejection of family involvement.
choices.feedback: The person may still want the sister involved in other parts of the plan. Ask what the person wants to share and verify any limits on confidentiality.

choices.label: Keep everything within the family discussion to honor the first request.
choices.feedback: That would deny the person a way to raise a new concern and could miss a duty the worker needs to address.

choices.label: Create a safe opportunity to respond privately, explain relevant limits and consult the authorized process about the specific concern.
choices.feedback: The worker preserves choice about family participation and attends to evidence and duties. Check whether the meeting can continue safely and what can be shared.

perspective: In this fictional case, the person sends a second message, “I want my sister here to discuss the schedule. Can you first tell me who has to hear what I say about safety?” What could the person need before deciding which details to share? What has the family actually been authorized to hear?
reconsider: A staff member with limited authority can still secure a private, accessible way for the person to speak and promptly involve the right decision maker.
followup: Record only the necessary information through the appropriate channel and confirm the next contact with the person.
reflection: Which part of this case would you need to verify before making a promise?
transfer: Write separate entries for the person’s request, the observed concern and the owner of a duty you need checked.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices
Minnesota · Person-centered, informed choice and transition protocol
Minnesota Statutes § 626.557, subdivisions 3, 4 and 4a — Reporting suspected maltreatment of vulnerable adults

title: Seeing through other eyes
objective: Respond to community distrust without defending the agency.
learn: How history shapes trust, including boarding schools and Tribal history, institutions for people with disabilities, and immigration enforcement.

teaching.title: Learn institutional history
teaching.text: The federal Indian boarding school investigation documents deliberate disruption of family, language and culture. Minnesota’s Governor’s Council on Developmental Disabilities describes the state’s history of institutional placement and movement toward community living. These are histories of government power. A staff member can learn them without asking a participant to supply a personal history.

teaching.title: Identify the present question
teaching.text: Past experiences can make a question about sharing information especially consequential. A federal study of services for unaccompanied children also documented concerns about disclosing immigration status in the settings it examined. That finding cannot tell you why a particular Minnesotan is asking who sees a form. Answer the person’s actual question.

teaching.title: Earn trust through a verifiable step
teaching.text: Give the most accurate answer you can about purpose, choice and access. Where you do not know the answer, identify who can establish it, offer a way to proceed safely within current rules and commit to a specific follow-up. A general promise of goodwill leaves the underlying question open.

scenario: A parent at a Minnesota information event asks, “If I sign in, who outside this office can see my name?” The facilitator wants to reassure everyone that DHS is here to help. The sign-in sheet gives no explanation.
decision: What should the facilitator do first?

choices.label: Explain that staff mean well and signing in is routine.
choices.feedback: Good intentions do not establish who can see the information or whether signing is required.

choices.label: Clarify the question, check the purpose and authorized access, and explain whether participation requires a name.
choices.feedback: This addresses the actual risk the person raised. If you cannot establish the answer immediately, say what can happen now and how you will follow up.

choices.label: Invite the parent to tell the group why they distrust government.
choices.feedback: A person should not have to disclose their history publicly to get an answer about data collection.

perspective: In this fictional case, the parent asks, “Could I see the information without putting my name on a sheet that other visitors can read?” That is the question the facilitator can answer or take to the person responsible. What could change a person’s decision about participating even if they never tell you why they asked?
reconsider: History should make staff more willing to hear a concern. An individual still owns the explanation for their own experience.
followup: Return the verified answer in the agreed form and correct the sign-in instructions if they failed to explain a real choice.
reflection: What public-facing process in your unit asks people to trust what they cannot see?
transfer: Write a two-line response that answers a question about information handling and names how you will verify anything uncertain.

sources.title: U.S. Department of the Interior · Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative investigation, 2024
Minnesota Governor’s Council on Developmental Disabilities · Forty-five years of history
U.S. Government Accountability Office · Unaccompanied Children, 2016
Eyal, Steffel and Epley · Perspective mistaking

title: Power in the room
objective: Reopen a decision so the people affected can shape it.
learn: Power differences between DHS and the people it serves and between leaders and staff, including who speaks, who decides and who bears the result.

teaching.title: Map power before sending an invitation
teaching.text: Write the question still open, who controls the decision, who bears a mistake and when change remains possible. If scope or funding has already been fixed, say so up front. People can then decide whether and how to spend time participating.

teaching.title: Watch what happens to specific evidence
teaching.text: A worker might hear a precise report about evening access and summarize it as “people want more flexibility.” The decision maker loses the detail needed to change staffing. Preserve the actionable point and let the contributor correct the summary without exposing unnecessary personal details.

teaching.title: Give an account of influence
teaching.text: A meaningful report-back says which options were considered, what changed and who will review the effect. If input could not alter a fixed element, explain the limit and whether another route exists. Attendance and satisfaction alone do not show that a decision was open.

scenario: A director presents a nearly final outreach schedule. Community attendees describe why a weekday morning site will be difficult. The contract fixes the site but the office can choose two additional hours. Attendees were told the entire plan was open.
decision: What would restore a real opportunity to influence the outcome?

choices.label: Clarify the fixed site and put the two hours back on the table with more than one way to contribute before the decision.
choices.feedback: Acknowledge the earlier overstatement. Give the group the criteria and a date for a decision and report-back.

choices.label: Thank everyone and include their comments in the minutes.
choices.feedback: A record is useful if the decision maker can still act on a concern. Minutes alone leave the actual options unclear.

choices.label: Promise to relocate regardless of the contract.
choices.feedback: A promise beyond the director’s current authority can undermine trust. The director can identify the contract owner and what change is feasible.

perspective: In this fictional case, a community participant says, “I rearranged work because the invitation said we could choose the location. If the site is set, which hours could we still change?” How would this invitation look to someone who paid for transportation and expected to help select the site?
reconsider: The same question applies inside DHS when leaders invite frontline staff after choices have already closed.
followup: Ask attendees whether their contribution reached the decision as intended and track the use of the added hours.
reflection: Which decision appears open on your team’s calendar after it has effectively closed?
transfer: Rewrite an invitation with the open decision, its limits, an accessible response route and a report-back date.

sources.title: Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams
Institute for Healthcare Improvement · Testing changes

title: Feedback across cultures
objective: Adapt feedback to direct and indirect styles while keeping one standard.
learn: Feedback as an ongoing conversation, including specific recognition, room for the employee's view and clear next steps.

teaching.title: Make feedback actionable
teaching.text: Describe the specific work, its consequence and the standard being applied. “When the callback time was missing, the next worker contacted the household during the wrong shift” gives a clearer basis for correction than a broad judgment about professionalism. Include specific recognition when the person’s work improved an outcome.

teaching.title: Invite the employee’s account
teaching.text: An employee may know that the system removed a note on transfer or that a supervisor gave conflicting instructions. Ask what happened on their side. Silence, fluent answers and confident delivery are all incomplete evidence of understanding. Offer time and a usable way to respond or correct the account.

teaching.title: Agree on a next check
teaching.text: Ask whether spoken, written or combined feedback would help the employee apply the same standard. State the agreed action, what support the supervisor owes and when you will review an example together. Honest, specific feedback gives a person access to growth and possible future opportunities.

scenario: A supervisor tells one analyst that a briefing lacked evidence. With a second analyst, the supervisor softens the same issue into “keep developing.” Neither the employee nor the review form names a specific change.
decision: How could the supervisor repair the difference?

choices.label: Use the same blunt wording with both employees.
choices.feedback: Identical delivery will not by itself identify the missing evidence, its consequence or the next opportunity to practice.

choices.label: Leave the second review positive to preserve trust.
choices.feedback: Withholding information the employee needs can make later decisions about readiness seem arbitrary.

choices.label: Share the same evidence standard, ask how each wants to receive feedback, and review the next draft against the stated criterion.
choices.feedback: This preserves a common expectation while making the information usable and giving both employees an opportunity to improve.

perspective: In this fictional case, the second analyst asks, “When you said to keep developing, I took a writing course. I still don't know which conclusion in my briefing needed more evidence.” If “keep developing” were the only feedback in your record, how would you know what would count as readiness for the next assignment?
reconsider: Adaptation can involve a different channel or pace. The evidence about the work still needs to be explicit.
followup: Check whether the employee can describe the intended change and whether the next example meets the agreed standard.
reflection: Who receives specific praise in your setting? Who receives only broad encouragement?
transfer: Write one observation, one question and one mutual commitment for a private feedback conversation.

sources.title: Eyal, Steffel and Epley · Perspective mistaking
Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams

title: Adapting without losing yourself
objective: Share the work of adapting across the whole team.
learn: When adapting builds trust and when it feels like imitation, and the cost of always being the one who adapts.

teaching.title: Identify who usually adjusts
teaching.text: Imagine a meeting where one employee repeatedly stays late to translate decisions for colleagues on a second shift. The arrangement may look cooperative to people who leave on time. Ask who routinely supplies extra explanation, travel or emotional effort, and which of those burdens can be shared.

teaching.title: Distinguish adaptation from imitation
teaching.text: A supervisor can ask whether written options, a slower turn-taking rhythm or a private conversation would help. Copying someone’s accent, mannerisms or presumed cultural habits can undermine respect. Start with a functional change that makes the decision usable and ask how it lands.

teaching.title: Make the adjustment reciprocal
teaching.text: Ask what the team can change, what the person wants to choose for themselves and how the outcome will be checked. The person can decline to take on an educator role. Document the shared method so success does not depend on one employee repeatedly absorbing the work.

scenario: A program analyst is always asked to explain colleagues’ feedback after meetings because others consider the analyst “good across cultures.” It takes hours, and the analyst’s own recommendations get less discussion.
decision: What should the manager try?

choices.label: Build a shared route for clarification into meetings, ask what the analyst wants to contribute and rotate follow-up duties.
choices.feedback: The team takes ownership of communication and the analyst can contribute their substantive work. Check whether the hidden workload actually falls.

choices.label: Give the analyst a team award and keep the arrangement.
choices.feedback: Recognition may matter, but it does not restore time or access to decisions.

choices.label: Forbid all informal follow-up after meetings.
choices.feedback: That could remove a useful avenue. The issue is who carries the work and which questions the meeting design leaves unanswered.

perspective: In this fictional case, the analyst tells the manager, “I'd like to present my own recommendation next week. When I spend the afternoon interpreting everyone's comments, I lose my preparation time.” What evidence would show the analyst again has time and influence in their own area of expertise?
reconsider: An adaptation deserves review when one person always does the adapting and others retain the original routine.
followup: Compare who owns follow-up work, how much time it takes and whether recommendations from all shifts receive a decision.
reflection: When have you mistaken someone’s willingness to help for unlimited capacity?
transfer: Describe one burden currently carried by an individual and one change the team can make within a month.

sources.title: Intercultural Development Continuum
Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams

title: Building teams across difference
objective: Run a fair hiring panel and sponsor staff from every background.
learn: Inclusive hiring, fair role design, and development and sponsorship, including for staff with disabilities.

teaching.title: Design around the actual work
teaching.text: Identify a realistic task, the judgment it requires and what competent performance looks like. A panel may overvalue polished oral answers when much of the job involves careful written analysis. Work with the appropriate hiring or human resources staff to use accessible, job-related methods within the applicable process.

teaching.title: Compare evidence before impressions
teaching.text: Give candidates the relevant expectations, invite appropriate access arrangements through the usual route and score the same decision criteria. Ask panelists to record specific observations before comparing impressions. A panel can then check whether availability, familiarity or confidence has become a substitute for demonstrated capability.

teaching.title: Examine the path into the pool
teaching.text: Sponsorship means using influence to give someone access to experience and recognition. Review who hears about projects, receives preparation and can take part across shifts or with disability-related access needs. A mentor can share advice; a supervisor with authority can change who gets assigned the work.

scenario: A hiring panel wants examples of cross-team coordination. A known candidate chaired several visible meetings. An evening employee coordinated handoffs during disruptions and can provide work samples. The advertised role also involves managing written handoffs.
decision: How should the panel compare evidence?

choices.label: Give preference to the candidate the panel has personally seen chairing meetings.
choices.feedback: Visibility alone does not show which coordination tasks the role requires or how well either candidate performed them.

choices.label: Score both against the stated coordination criteria, ask comparable follow-up questions, and record the basis for the selection.
choices.feedback: The panel can compare the quality of evidence across settings. Separately, a supervisor can widen future access to visible stretch work.

choices.label: Select the less visible candidate to correct the earlier opportunity gap.
choices.feedback: The gap matters. The decision still requires job-related evidence under the actual selection process, alongside work to improve the pipeline.

perspective: In this fictional case, the evening applicant says, “I wrote the handoff that kept the services running. Someone else presented the work at the daytime briefing. Can I walk you through my decisions?” Which tasks might demonstrate leadership for a person who uses a different communication method or works outside a manager’s line of sight?
reconsider: Inclusive role design begins before interviews. Check whether the stated duty requires the ability the panel plans to test.
followup: Review which task evidence predicted success and which staff gained new preparation opportunities afterward.
reflection: Who can currently demonstrate the skills your panel says it prizes?
transfer: Write a criterion, two comparable ways to demonstrate it and one sponsorship action available in your role.

sources.title: Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams
Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices

title: Designing services that adapt
objective: Lead a review of a policy or notice with community input and report back.
learn: The National CLAS Standards, language access, person-centered planning and co-design with communities.

teaching.title: Begin with the decision people face
teaching.text: Ask a reader what they think the notice requires, which options they can see and what they would do next. A signature or readability score does not establish those things. Include people who previously could not complete the step as well as people who completed it successfully.

teaching.title: Distinguish wording, language and access
teaching.text: Plain words help, but may not address a requested language, screen-reader order or a deadline that arrives before help is available. Determine which language access and accessibility responsibilities apply with the right owner. For disability supports, ask the person how they want to understand and direct their next decision.

teaching.title: Co-design a change and report back
teaching.text: Tell contributors what can change, who will approve a version and how they can participate. Ask them to compare two formats on the actual task. Track the effort required from readers and staff, revise the notice, then share what you changed and why a suggestion could or could not be used.

scenario: A unit tests a shorter notice. Readers can repeat its first sentence yet several still miss the option to ask for a different appointment. A compliance reviewer says the statement about timing must remain.
decision: What change would provide the most useful test?

choices.label: Remove the timing statement and see if comprehension improves.
choices.feedback: That could change an actual requirement. Ask the responsible owner what must remain and test an approved design.

choices.label: Ask only long-time staff to proofread the next draft.
choices.feedback: Staff can verify content but may already know where every option is, unlike someone reading for the first time.

choices.label: Keep the verified timing and test whether readers can find, choose and act on the appointment option in an accessible version.
choices.feedback: A concrete task exposes whether the design works. Include requested languages and formats, then check that testing did not create extra costs for the reader.

perspective: In this fictional case, a reader comments, “I can tell you the appointment date. I still can't find where I would ask for another time without losing the appointment.” What could someone repeat accurately while still lacking enough information to make a choice?
reconsider: Ask what the person wants help with before treating an easier-to-read notice as a successful service outcome.
followup: Tell contributors which version was chosen and compare successful next steps and repeat contacts after a limited rollout.
reflection: Whose experience would disappear if you evaluated your next notice only by total calls?
transfer: Write a task for a notice test and a report-back sentence explaining how readers’ findings will reach the decision maker.

sources.title: HHS Office of Minority Health · National CLAS Standards
Minnesota DHS · Person-centered practices
Institute for Healthcare Improvement · Testing changes

title: The leader as bridge
objective: Help two groups that blame each other agree on one shared action.
learn: How to mediate between programs and between DHS and communities, and how to respect Tribal sovereignty by working through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

teaching.title: Translate the handoff
teaching.text: One program may say referrals are incomplete while another says the receiving unit never calls back. Trace a single fictional referral from both sides. Identify what each team could see, when they knew action was needed and who had authority to correct a gap. Preserve each group’s account where they differ.

teaching.title: Distinguish kinds of partnership
teaching.text: A community organization may describe service experience and a county partner may control an operational step. A Tribal Nation has a government-to-government relationship with the state. When state action may affect a Tribal Nation, engage the responsible Tribal relations staff and applicable consultation process. A personal connection cannot confer authority to speak for a Nation.

teaching.title: Agree on the smallest joint action
teaching.text: Ask each group what it can change without waiting on the other. Then choose one shared action, a responsible person on each side, a date to compare evidence and a way for affected people to say whether service improved. A bridge fails when the person using the service must carry messages indefinitely.

scenario: A community partner says a referral line drops families. Program staff say partners send referrals without a requested contact method. A director proposes a meeting about attitudes. Both groups can pilot a confirmation message through approved channels.
decision: What agreement should the leader seek?

choices.label: Trace a de-identified handoff, test a confirmed contact method and receipt, and set a joint review date.
choices.feedback: This shows what each side needs to see. Check with people using the route before assuming a staff confirmation equals a successful connection.

choices.label: Ask the community partner to take responsibility for every failed referral.
choices.feedback: This assumes where the failure occurs and could push more work onto the people with the least control over the line.

choices.label: Promise that the state will adopt the partner’s process everywhere.
choices.feedback: That goes beyond a small test and may exceed the director’s authority. Identify who could authorize broader changes after evidence is available.

perspective: In this fictional case, a person using the service explains, “I was told that my referral had been sent. When no one called, I couldn't tell who had it or which office to ask.” Which part of the handoff can only the person seeking help tell you about?
reconsider: If a Tribal government is involved, identify the government relationship and the authorized contact before proposing a shared operational test.
followup: Compare completed connections, time to usable contact and any repeat storytelling the new step requires.
reflection: Where has your unit treated a relationship issue as if it could be solved entirely by better forms?
transfer: Write a three-party handoff statement identifying the two owners and what the person seeking service should experience.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes §10.65 · Government-to-government relationship with Tribal governments
Institute for Healthcare Improvement · Testing changes

title: Capstone: Leading intercultural change
objective: Write a personal leadership plan, rehearse teaching one course idea and practice mentoring a leader earlier in the series.
learn: Bring the series together by explaining what you now notice, what you do differently and which system change you can test. The teach-back and mentoring exercise can both be completed independently.

teaching.title: Choose a consequential decision
teaching.text: Identify whose opportunity or service is affected, whose evidence currently reaches the decision and who can act. State a baseline you could actually observe. Separate what your data establish from the explanation you suspect. In a fictional project, mark all numbers and outcomes as hypothetical.

teaching.title: Write a SMART aim and a PDSA test
teaching.text: A SMART aim is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. A short test uses Plan, Do, Study, Act. For example, test a second route for shift workers over two openings. Plan how to record timely receipt; try the route; compare actual reach with your prediction; keep, change or end the test. Include a check for extra workload.

teaching.title: Teach and mentor through a rehearsal
teaching.text: Choose one course idea and record or write a two-minute explanation for an imagined team. Then write a response to an aspiring leader who says, “I can see the barrier, but I cannot change the rule.” Ask for an observation, identify an action within their authority and name the owner for the larger change. A real teach-back or mentoring conversation is optional.

scenario: A fictional unit counted acting assignments last year and found all went to employees on the day shift. People on both shifts have relevant responsibilities. The unit cannot tell who saw the openings or what evidence each applicant could submit.
decision: Which proposed first cycle produces the strongest learning?

choices.label: Require the next appointment to go to evening staff and announce success.
choices.feedback: One result would not reveal who knew in time, what evidence was considered or whether the opportunity stayed accessible. Check authority before making any selection commitment.

choices.label: For the next two openings, test notice on both shifts, compare timely receipt and review submitted evidence against stated criteria.
choices.feedback: This tests an actionable barrier. Add a private way to report missed access, monitor extra work and decide who can revise the next cycle.

choices.label: Wait for a full workforce assessment before altering the process.
choices.feedback: Broader evidence can help, but a small reversible test can answer an immediate question without assigning scores or labels to employees.

perspective: In this fictional case, an evening employee tells the project lead, “I can show you how I handled a difficult handoff. I first need to know an opening exists while I still have a shift to prepare.” Write one sentence each from the perspective of an aspiring leader, the selection owner and an employee who never received the first notice. Which claim would require you to ask them directly?
reconsider: Revisit one earlier lesson. Explain which decision you would change now and what other reasonable explanation you still need to test.
followup: Review your plan against four checks: a person can influence a real decision, the action fits the owner’s authority, the measure captures usable access, and someone will respond if the result disappoints.
reflection: What do you now notice, what do you do differently, and which institutional habit are you prepared to test next?
transfer: Save a one-page personal plan with your SMART aim, PDSA cycle, teach-back, mentoring response, first review date and a go/change/stop rule. You can complete it without sharing personal data or scheduling a live activity.

Intercultural Development Continuum
Nembhard and Edmondson · Leader inclusiveness and professional status in health care teams
